                  Mind the rank! Finite-resource effects in quantum linear regression
                   Surprises in Quantum Linear Regression with Finite Resources
                        Gabriele Lo Monaco ,1, ∗ Salvatore Lorenzo ,1 Alessandro Ferraro ,2
                        Mauro Paternostro ,1, 3 G. Massimo Palma ,1 and Luca Innocenti 1
      1 Università degli Studi di Palermo, Dipartimento di Fisica e Chimica - Emilio Segrè, via Archirafi 36, I-90123 Palermo, Italy

      2 Quantum Technology Lab, Dipartimento di Fisica Aldo Pontremoli, Università degli Studi di Milano, I-20133 Milano, Italy

                               3 Centre for Quantum Materials and Technologies, School of Mathematics
                                and Physics, Queen’s University Belfast, BT7 1NN, United Kingdom
              Quantum linear regression offers a non-variational approach to quantum machine learning, yet its
              behavior under realistic measurement constraints remains poorly understood. Focusing on quan-
              tum extreme learning machines, we analyze their performance when the feature probabilities of each
              training state are estimated from only N measurements. A key observation is that the ideal probabil-
              ity matrix has rank at most the square of the Hilbert space dimension of the measured states, whereas
              its finite-shot counterpart is full rank with high probability. As a result, the pseudoinverse diverges
              for large N, and in particular the finite-shot pseudoinverse does not converge to the ideal Moore–
              Penrose pseudoinverse. Leveraging tools from random matrix theory and concentration inequalities,
              we show that these divergences can be controlled and derive the leading behavior of the test error, up
              to corrections that are small with high probability. We prove that the test error contains a bias term
              scaling as N −2 , while fluctuations over realizations of the training shot noise are characterized by a
              training variance scaling as ( Nntr )−1 . Although the additional singular directions are projected out
              when the training targets and test probabilities are exact, we show that noise in the targets features
              can couple to these directions and amplify the variance arising from finite test statistics. These results
              establish a resource tradeoff between the dataset size and the number of measurements per state, and
              provide a baseline for resource-aware training and regularization strategies.

shown.                                                          bias–variance decomposition of the mean-squared pre-
                                                                diction error, first at fixed noise realization and then af-
                                                                ter averaging over noise using standard concentration
                                                                arguments. A key outcome is that the dominant contri-
                                                                butions exhibit distinct and operationally meaningful
                                                                scalings: the squared bias term can persist even in the
                                                                quantum analogue of the underparametrized regime
                                                                (ntr > nout ) and scales as N −2 , whereas the variance
                                                                scales as ( Nntr )−1 . These behaviors highlight a trade-
                                                                off that departs from classical intuition: increasing the
                                                                number of training states is not necessarily beneficial
                                                                if the per-state measurement budget is too small, be-
                                                                cause the irreducible bias induced by rank-increasing
                                                                noise cannot be mitigated by more data alone.
                                                                Beyond the specific QELM setting, our results sug-
                                                                gest a broader lesson for quantum machine learning:

                                                SM1.             PRELIMINARIES

We use the following linear-algebra notation throughout the main text and the Supplemental Material. Lowercase
bold letters, such as v, denote vectors, with components vk , whereas uppercase bold letters, such as M, denote
matrices. This section also fixes the common coordinate system used by the two pseudoinverse analyses later in
the SM. Section SM1.1 translates operators and operator collections into real vectors and matrices, section SM1.2
reviews the Landau notation for deterministic sequences and sequences of random variables used in the main text
and the appendix, section SM1.3 introduces the signal, kernel, and cokernel blocks of the ideal probability matrix,
and section SM1.4 records the pseudoinverse identities used throughout sections SM2 and SM3.


                                               SM1.1.            Vectorized notation

This subsection connects the operator language of quantum states, POVMs, and frames with the real matrix coor-
dinates used in all subsequent calculations. In particular, it makes the frame operators of section SM1.5 and the
probability-matrix blocks of section SM1.3 part of one consistent notation. Given a Hilbert space H of dimension d,
let L (H) denote its space of linear operators, equipped with the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product ⟨ A, B⟩ = Tr A† B .
                                                                                                                    
Our coordinate matrices represent the real Hilbert space Herm(H) ⊂ L (H)using a Hermitian orthonormal basis;
hence its dimension is d2 , its coordinate vectors are real, and matrix adjoints reduce to transposes. Ordinary upper-
case Roman and Greek letters denote operators. For a vector ψ ∈ H, we write P(ψ) = Pψ ≡ |ψ⟩ ⟨ψ|. We also use the
same symbol for the rank-one superoperator generated by A ∈ L (H):
                                                                                         
                           P( A) : L (H) → L (H),         P( A)( B) ≡ ⟨ A, B⟩ A = Tr A† B A.                     (SM1)

This superoperator is an orthogonal projector when ⟨ A, A⟩ = 1; otherwise it is the corresponding unnormalized
rank-one outer product.
                                                             2
Given a Hermitian orthonormal operator basis (Pi )id=1 (for example, normalized Pauli operators), any O ∈ Herm(H)
has the real vectorized representation vO = vec(O) and (vO )i = Tr Pi† O . Collections of Hermitian operators are
                                                                             
denoted by bold Greek letters, as in the POVM µ = (µ a )ma=1 . Such a collection is represented by the matrix
                                                       m                 m
                                            M µ ≡ ∑ vµa e Ta = ∑ vec(µ a )e Ta ,                                   (SM2)
                                                      a =1              a =1

where e a is the ath canonical basis vector of Rm .


                                              SM1.2.             Asymptotic notation

Several results below concern the asymptotic behavior of the shot-noise matrix as ntr → ∞. For deterministic quan-
tities, we use the standard Landau notation, with the subscript indicating the variable with respect to which the
asymptotic limit is taken. Thus, for instance, an = on (bn ) means
                                                 an
                                                    −→ 0               as n → ∞,
                                                 bn
while an = On (bn ) means that | an /bn | remains bounded as n → ∞. When the asymptotic variable is clear from the
context, we may omit the subscript and simply write o (bn ) and O(bn ).
                                                                                       P
For a generic sequence of random variables ( Ẑn )n , we write Ẑn = oP (1), or Ẑn −→ 0, if, for every η > 0, P(| Ẑn | >
                                                                             P
η ) → 0 as n → ∞. More generally, Ẑn = oP ( an ) means Ẑn /an −→ 0, whereas Ẑn = OP ( an ) means that the sequence
( Ẑn /an )n is bounded in probability.

                                                            SM1.4.      Properties of pseudoinverses

This final notational subsection collects the pseudoinverse facts needed to turn the block decomposition of sec-
tion SM1.3 into the formal expansion of section SM2. It also fixes the projector identities used later in the direct and
probabilistic arguments.
                                                                                                                                    S4

Definition via SVD — The pseudoinverse of a rectangular matrix is most conveniently expressed through its compact
singular value decomposition (SVD). Given a matrix A, write A = U DV † , where U, V are isometries and D > 0 is
diagonal. Its pseudoinverse then reads A+ = V D −1 U † . If A is n × m, then U is n × r, D is r × r, and V is m × r,
where r ≡ rank( A). In dyadic notation, this amounts to A = ∑k dk uk v†k having pseudoinverse A+ = ∑k d−  1    †
                                                                                                         k vk uk .

Properties of the pseudoinverse — The pseudoinverse A+ is a true (left and right) inverse iff A is invertible. More
generally, A+ is a left inverse, A+ A = I, if and only if A is injective, and it is a right inverse, AA+ = I, if and
only if A is surjective. If A is not full-rank, then A+ is neither a left nor a right inverse, but it can still be seen as an
inverse on the range of support of A. In general, A+ A = Πsupp( A) is the orthogonal projector onto the row space of
A, whereas AA+ = Πim( A) projects onto its image.
Explicit formulas for special cases — The pseudoinverse can be given an explicit formula when A is injective or surjec-
tive. For injective A, we have A+ = ( A† A)−1 A† . For surjective A, we have A+ = A† ( AA† )−1 .
Product formulas — It is not generally the case that ( AB)+ = B+ A+ . However, it does hold when A is injective and B
is surjective. Indeed, the compact SVD of B is B = U B D B V †B , with U B unitary, whereas that of A is A = U A D A V †A ,
with V A unitary. Therefore

                                                  AB = U A D A V †A U B D B V †B ,                                              (SM8)

where V †A U B is unitary and D A , D B are square and invertible. Hence C ≡ D A V †A U B D B is also square and invertible.
                   †
Let C = U C DC V C   be its SVD. Then

                                                  AB = (U A U C ) DC (V B V C )†                                                (SM9)

is an SVD for AB, with U C , V C unitaries, hence

                                     ( AB)+ = (V B V C ) DC−1 (U A U C )† = V B C −1 U †A ,                                    (SM10)

which equals B+ A+ .

                                                                                                   

                                               −( M/A)−1 CA−1          ( M/A)−1
                                                                                                                               (SM11)
                                               ( M/D )−1           −( M/D )−1 BD −1

                                  ( M/A) ≡ D − CA−1 B,                ( M/D ) ≡ A − BD −1 C.                                   (SM12)

The first representation assumes that A is invertible, whereas the second assumes that D is invertible. This identity
is used by both the complementary structural analysis and the direct proof below.


                                                    SM1.5.       Frame operators

This section supplies the frame-theoretic bridge between quantum measurements and the regression coefficients
used later in section SM4. We introduce frames, their canonical duals, and their frame operators, and then specialize
these constructions to state ensembles and POVMs. The symmetric-design identities derived at the end of the section
are the ingredients used to evaluate the leading resource coefficients in section SM4.3. We make frequent use of
frames and frame operators [56–58]. For a finite-dimensional inner-product space V, a frame is a collection (vk )k ⊂ V
for which

                                                α∥w∥2 ≤ ∑ |⟨vk , w⟩|2 ≤ β∥w∥2                                                  (SM13)
                                                             k
                                                                                                                        S5

for some 0 < α ≤ β < ∞. Frames generalize orthonormal bases by allowing overcompleteness. Given any dual
frame (ṽk )k , every w ∈ V admits the reconstructions

                                             w = ∑⟨vk , w⟩ṽk = ∑⟨ṽk , w⟩vk .                                     (SM14)
                                                   k               k

The canonical dual is ṽk = F −1 (vk ), where the positive, invertible frame operator is F = ∑k vk v†k . An overcomplete
frame has nonunique duals.
The frame operator Fρ ≡ M ρ M ρT associated with the training set ρ and the frame operator Fµ ≡ M µ M µT associated
with the POVM µ are intimately related to the probability matrix P ≡ ⟨µ, ρ⟩ ≡ M µT M ρ . In particular, this relation
naturally emerges by looking at their singular values. The singular values of the probability matrix are by definition
the square roots of the eigenvalues of PP T = M µT M ρ M ρT M µ that in turn are the same as the nonzero eigenvalues of
M ρ M ρT M µ M µT = Fρ Fµ . We therefore conclude that the nonzero singular values of P are equal to the square roots
of the nonzero eigenvalues of Fµ Fρ .
Case of symmetric states and measurement — In particular, if the training states are pure, ρk = P(ψk ), and form a
complex-projective 2-design, then in superoperator notation
                                                       ntr
                                                                       Id +P( I )
                                            Fρ ≡ ∑ P(ρk ) = ntr                    ,                               (SM15)
                                                   k =1
                                                                        d ( d + 1)

where Id is the identity superoperator and P( I )( X ) = Tr( X ) I, with I the identity operator on H. Note that, as a
linear operator, this Fρ has eigenvalues ndtr and d(dn+
                                                      tr
                                                         1)
                                                            , with degeneracies 1 and d2 − 1, respectively. If the training
states are independent Haar-random pure states, then their normalized empirical frame operator approaches this
form with high probability as ntr grows. Similarly, symmetric rank-one POVMs have the form µb = nout         d
                                                                                                                P(ϕb ) with
                            nout         nout
the states |ϕb ⟩ such that ∑b=1 P(ϕb ) = d I. If these states further form a complex-projective 2-design, then the

The eigenvector corresponding to ntr /nout is the rescaled identity, I/ d, while the other eigenvalue has degeneracy

                                SM2.   PERTURBATIVE PSEUDOINVERSE EXPANSION

In this section we present a perturbative analysis of the pseudoinverse of the empirical probability matrix. More
generally, we consider the pseudoinverse of a rectangular singular matrix subject to a generally full-rank pertur-
bation. The main results are the expansions in eqs. (SM30) and (SM32). Here we focus only on the mathematical
structure of the perturbative expansion. This formal calculation explains which blocks become singular when shot
noise changes the rank. The independent direct analysis in section SM3 then establishes uniform probabilistic control
of the prediction error, and section SM4 translates that rigorous control into training-resource statements.
                                                                                                                                  S6

The main technical difficulty is that matrix inversion is not continuous with respect to perturbations that change the
rank, and the same is true for the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse [33, 34, 52]. Let P be the unperturbed matrix and
let P̂τ = P + τ Ξ̂. Here τ is a generic parameter; we will use τ = N −1/2 when specializing the discussion to the
empirical frequency matrix. If P is rank deficient and the perturbation Ξ̂ has components outside the row or column
                         +                                                  +
spaces of P, then τ 7→ P̂τ is discontinuous at τ = 0, and in particular P̂τ can diverge as τ → 0. More precisely,
when the perturbation changes the rank, one has the lower bound [34]
                                                              +                 1
                                                          ∥P̂τ − P+ ∥op ≥            .                                        (SM19)
                                                                            τ ∥Ξ̂∥op
For finite-dimensional matrices, continuity of the pseudoinverse is equivalent to the rank being stable under the
perturbation. However, the stochastic setting considered here generally does cause the rank to increase, being P
has rank at most d2 , while shot noise makes P̂ have maximal rank min(ntr , nout ) with high probability. Here and
throughout, ∥ · ∥op denotes the spectral norm, i.e. the largest singular value.
To illustrate the structural effect of eq. (SM11), suppose now that a symmetric singular matrix M undergoes a rank-
increasing perturbation M τ ≡ M + τX, and let x ∈ supp( M ) and y ∈ im( M ). In a basis adapted to supp( M ) ⊕
ker( M ), we can write these variables more explicitly as

We assume throughout that the empirical matrix is wide, ntr ≥ nout , and has full row rank after perturbation. The

model, the probability of P̂ N and Ξ̂22 not having full row rank is technically nonzero, but decreases exponentially
fast with ntr . The argument in section SM3 takes this into account showing that even the unlikely events where the
empirical matrix is extremely ill-conditioned do not affect the overall averaged MSE. Under these conditions, the

                           SM3.    DIRECT PROOF: BIAS, LINEAR FLUCTUATION, AND REMAINDER

This section contains the proof of the MSE and resource-scaling result stated in section VI, and is logically in-
dependent of the formal small-τ expansion in section SM2. Both analyses use the exact wide-matrix identity
  +     T     T
P̂ = P̂ (P̂ P̂ )−1 when P̂ has full row rank, and the block inverse formula eq. (SM11), but none of the truncated
expansions eqs. (SM30) and (SM32) is used below. Instead, we first eliminate the rank-increasing directions by an ex-
act Schur complement and only then expand the resulting well-conditioned d2 × d2 matrix. This order of operations
enables a uniform high-probability bound on the remainder.
In section SM3.1, we prove a decomposition ∆ô = B + L̂ + R̂ of the infinite-test-statistics error ∆ô into a determin-
istic component B, a centered fluctuation L̂, and a remainder R̂. We identify the deterministic bias component B
                                                                                                                                                         S9

in section SM3.2. In section SM3.3 we derive the form of the fluctuation term L̂, show that it has zero average, and
compute its variance. We then prove in section SM3.4 that the remainder R̂ is subleading, conditionally on a stochas-
tic event where the pseudoinverses are sufficiently well-conditioned. In section SM3.5 we then prove that this event
has high probability for large ntr . To conclude the bound on the MSE we only need to make sure that the stochastic
events in which pseudoinverses are ill-conditioned do not make the MSE explode. We do this in section SM3.6,
where we show that the divergence of R̂ in the exceptional realizations does not overcome the exponentially small
probability of these events. This concludes the proof and provides us with an unconditional MSE bound for large
ntr . A summary of the the notation used in the proof is given in table SM1.

Theorem 3 (High-probability remainder bound). For fixed d and nout , there are deterministic constants u⋆ , CR , C0 > 0,
                                                                                                                              r2
independent of N and ntr , such that for any δ satisfying C0 rδ ≤ u⋆ , with probability at least 1 − δ, we have | R̂| ≤ CR √δ .
                                                                                                                               N

Proof. The proof combines the probabilistic control of the basic fluctuations with the deterministic remainder esti-
mate. Specifically, corollary 1 places all the required blocks and vectors in an event of the form Eu with probability
at least 1 − δ. Once its tolerance u is below a fixed threshold, eqs. (SM74) to (SM75) guarantee both invertibility and
the quadratic remainder bound.
Choose C0 ≥ max{1, KS } as in corollary 1, and recall the definition of rδ from eq. (SM77). Thus the event EC0 rδ
happens with probability at least 1 − δ. Choose u⋆ > 0, independent on N, such that u⋆ ≤ 1, u⋆ ≤ κ22 /2, and
                                                                                                                                    S17

 p
KS u⋆ + KSnl u2⋆ ≤ κeff /2. Then, for all N ≥ 1 and u ≤ u⋆ , the conditions of eq. (SM74) are satisfied, and thus
                √
| R̂| ≤ K R u2 / N holds with probability at least 1 − δ.
Suppose now that δ is such that C0 rδ ≤ u⋆ . Then P(EC0 rδ ) ≥ 1 − δ, and also the conditions of eq. (SM74) are satisfied
                                             √            √
with u = C0 rδ . Thus | R̂| ≤ K R (C0 rδ )2 / N = CR rδ2 / N, where CR ≡ K R C02 .

To convert the condition C0 rδ ≤ u⋆ into a condition on ntr , observe that
Unpacking   the definition of rδ with eq. (SM77), we see that C0 rδ ≤ u⋆ is equivalent to ntr ≥ qδ /c⋆ where c⋆ ≡
( 1 + 4(u⋆ /C0 ) − 1)2 /4. And plugging in qδ , this amounts to ntr ≥ (2nout log 9 + log(32/δ))/c⋆ . Thus, the high
 p

probability bound of theorem 3 holds for ntr ≳ nout + log(1/δ). For every fixed confidence level 1 − δ and fixed nout ,
this condition therefore holds for all sufficiently large ntr . At fixed ntr , taking δ arbitrarily close to zero increases qδ
and can violate the condition; this makes the bound inconclusive, but does not assert that the empirical matrices are
singular.

                                       SM4.      COST SCALING OF TRAINING A QELM

The goal of this section is to translate the rigorous error expansion of section SM3 into a resource-cost statement
for QELM training, focusing on the number of training states and shots per state. Section SM4.1 rewrites the exact
bias and variance coefficients in frame language, section SM4.2 converts their asymptotic limits into the dataset-
size/shot-budget tradeoff, and section SM4.3 evaluates the resulting leading coefficients for symmetric tight designs.
Thus this section is the application layer connecting the direct probabilistic theorem to the resource statements high-
lighted in the main text.
Problem setting and notation — Suppose that every state in the training set is measured N times. Because shot noise
generally makes the target rows inconsistent with the row space of the observed frequency matrix, QELM training
is naturally formulated as the least-squares problem
                                                                                          2
                                                                         T
                                               Ŵ O ∈ arg min W P̂ N − M O Mρ                  .                         (SM113)
                                                             W                            F


Here P̂ N is the noisy probability matrix, whose k-th column contains the frequencies obtained from N measurements
                                                                   n
of ρk , and P = E[P̂ N ] = ⟨µ, ρ⟩ = M µT M ρ . Furthermore, M O = ∑i=obs1 vec(Oi ) ⟨i | is the matrix whose columns are the
                                                                                                                         S21

                                               n
vectorized target observables O ≡ {Oi }i=obs1 , and similarly M ρ = ∑in=tr1 vec(ρi ) ⟨i | describes the (vectorized) training
                                                                                         +
states ρ ≡ {ρi }in=tr1 . The canonical least-squares solution is Ŵ O = ⟨O , ρ⟩P̂ N .
Training with infinite statistics — At infinite training statistics, P̂ N is replaced by its expectation P. Under the com-
pleteness assumptions stated below, the noiseless least-squares residual vanishes, and the canonical solution is
                                             T
                                     W O = (MO M ρ )( M µT M ρ )+ = M O
                                                                      T
                                                                        M µT + = ⟨O , µ̃⟩.                          (SM114)
This result assumes that both M ρ and M µ have full row rank: physically this amounts to the training states being
complete — i.e., spanning the space of all Hermitian operators — and the POVM being informationally complete.
Under this assumption, the pseudoinverse of the product also factorises as ( M µT M ρ )+ = M +            T+
                                                                                                      ρ M µ . Furthermore,
it is a general fact that the pseudoinverse of a surjective matrix can be interpreted as the transpose of the matrix
representing the canonical dual frame of the frame given by the columns of the original matrix. Formally, this means
that M +            T
        µ = ( M µ̃ ) . For more details on this perspective, we refer to the discussion in [15, 59]. In conclusion, training
with infinite statistics amounts to recovering a description of the POVM µ through its dual µ̃.
Using Ŵ rather than Ŵ O — From eq. (SM113), the canonical solution depends linearly on O through M O . This
means that the training is not really about the training observables O per se, but rather provides a reconstruction of
the POVM itself. For the cost analysis it is therefore convenient to use the canonical solution:
                                                                                         +
                                              Ŵ = min ∥W P̂ N − M ρ ∥2 = M ρ P̂ N .                                (SM115)
                                                       W

This amounts to using the training to find an estimator for the states themselves, rather than for any specific observ-
able. Estimators for target observables can then be recovered afterwards by simply multiplying by the observables
                               T
we are interested in: Ŵ O = M O Ŵ. This perspective also highlights the fact that the cost of training does not depend
on the number of target observables, per se. Specializing the training to a specific target observable is a simple matter
of post-processing and does not affect the measurement stage at all.

                                                 SM4.2.      Resource scaling

Section SM4.1 identifies the finite-N frame coefficients and their N → ∞ limits. We now insert them into the rigorous
MSE expansion to expose which error terms are controlled by shots per state and which are controlled by the total
number of measured training copies. This is the resource conclusion used in the main text. First, substituting the
finite-N coefficients from eq. (SM116) into eq. (SM112) expresses the two leading terms as b2N /N 2 and VN /( Nntr ).
Then using b N = b + O( N −1 ) and VN = V + O( N −1 ), with the limiting coefficients in eq. (SM119), gives

                                   b2N                          b2
                                                                                              
                               2         VN                           V                      1
                       EΞ̂ [∆ô ] = 2 +       + O(Err N,ntr ) = 2 +       + O Err N,ntr + 3 ,                (SM120)
                                   N     Nntr                  N     Nntr                  N

with Err N,ntr defined in eq. (SM111). The additional N −3 term comes from replacing b2N by b2 ; the N-dependence
                                                                                                             −1
of VN is already absorbed by Err N,ntr . Note that the N −3 correction is retained because Err N,ntr is O(ntr   ) for large
           −  3                                       − 2   −1
ntr , and N need not be smaller than terms like N ntr when ntr > N. At fixed d and nout , the leading variance
is controlled by the total number Ntot = Nntr of measured training copies, whereas the squared bias is controlled
by the number of shots per state. If |b| and V remain bounded above and away from zero, increasing ntr at fixed N
suppresses the variance but leaves the bias floor b2 /N 2 , and the crossover occurs at ntr ≍ N. The bias originates from
the deterministic N −1 Σeff shift induced by the rank-increasing shot noise; the variance originates from the centered
first-order fluctuation.

which is independent of ntr . The bound also holds with probability tending to one for independent Haar-random

The smallest eigenvalue of the limiting operator is 1/[d(d + 1)]. Consequently, for example, λmin (Fρ /ntr ) ≥

frame bound for Haar-random training designs with probability tending to one. The block dimensions and the
identity r = d2 are those of section SM1.3.

In an orthonormal basis that diagonalizes Q̂, the nonzero part of the centered matrix in this display consists of

It remains to justify the claimed conditional independence. In the Schur complement, the contribution from the
                                             +
centered Ξ̂12 block is right-multiplied by Ξ̂22 Ξ̂21 and hence depends only on its projection onto the row space of Ξ̂22 .
By contrast, the Wishart matrix in the preceding display depends only on its projection onto ker(Ξ̂22 ). These two
projections are orthogonal, since
                                                                +
                                                             (Ξ̂22 Ξ̂22 ) Q̂ = 0.

The centered Ξ̂12 block is matrix normal with identity column covariance, so its two orthogonal projections have
zero cross-covariance and, being jointly Gaussian, are independent. The centered Ξ̂11 block appearing in the Schur
complement is independent of both because it consists of different columns. This proves the conditional indepen-
dence of the two matrices in the lemma. Finally, the mean of a Wishart matrix is its number of degrees of freedom
times its scale, which gives eq. (SM136).

the lower blocks proves that the two contractions have zero covariance.

                                                    SM6.        NUMERICAL RESULTS

In this section, we present several numerical simulations supporting the theoretical discussion in the manuscript.
All simulations estimate the training bias and variance numerically using a finite number of realizations of the shot
noise arising during training or testing. Achieving full agreement between the simulations and the theoretical results
therefore requires unbiased estimators of the bias and variance. This subtlety is discussed in detail in section SM6.1.
The numerical simulations serve two distinct purposes. First, we explore a range of settings to demonstrate the broad
applicability of the manuscript’s theoretical findings. For example, in section SM6.3, we reproduce the predicted
scaling of the MSE, bias, and variance for randomly generated POVMs. Second, the simulations in section SM6.2
provide empirical evidence supporting the validity of the Gaussian approximation discussed in the main text.


                              SM6.1.      Unbiased estimators for the training bias and variance

The bias–variance decomposition in eqs. (12) and (18) is defined in terms of exact averages over the shot noise. In the
simulations, the average over p̂σ is performed analytically using eq. (12) while the average over the training noise is
replaced by a finite sample mean. We derive the resulting estimators at fixed training set, POVM, observable O , and
test state σ; any further average over these objects is performed only afterwards.
For each realization of the training shot-noise, let
